Dialogue-based task-oriented reinforcement learning can inadvertently degrade lexical diversity, as models tend to converge on a limited set of words that maximize rewards. This study presents an approach to enhancing lexical diversity in such contexts by integrating future prediction into the reward function. Specifically, it introduces a new reward formulation grounded in mean-squared prediction error (MSPPE) of the model's own outputs. Furthermore, the model incorporates an attentional mechanism to selectively focus on the most relevant upcoming turns. Experimental results indicate that this method effectively boosts lexical diversity without compromising performance.

Ten years after Wilson's Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) paper, we have witnessed the emergence of the lattice approach, which has become a pivotal area of study. This method, initially proposed by Kenneth Wilson for exploring the non-perturbative components of QCD, relies on numerical simulations and was designed to address phenomena that standard perturbation theory cannot adequately capture. Lattice QCD is currently the sole viable approach for investigating the non-perturbative dynamics of QCD, particularly in the low-energy regime, and has been instrumental in deriving the QCD mass scale, calculating strong coupling constants, and analyzing hadronic spectra. This tutorial provides an overview of the subject for those unfamiliar with it, beginning with an introduction to the Lattice approach and its fundamental principles. Subsequently, we examine the QCD action, detailing how hadrons and quarks are incorporated into the formalism. Finally, the text outlines strategies for QCD calculations involving baryons and mesons, and discusses the challenges associated with the fermion doubling problem.

Accurate prediction of load responses is essential for condition monitoring and fault detection on offshore wind turbines. This study introduces a novel, robust prediction framework that leverages multivariate sparse kernel regression combined with optimized sparsifying transforms. By addressing the class imbalance between frequent low-load states and rare high-load events, the sparsifying transform effectively models the heteroscedastic nature of load data. To further enhance prediction precision, the method incorporates a new loss function grounded in the statistical characteristics of load responses. Additionally, the proposed neural network is strengthened through a hybrid training strategy that integrates both $l_1$ and $l_2$ regularization terms. Experimental results across three datasets, benchmarked against multiple existing methods, demonstrate that the developed kernel regression model achieves superior performance.

This paper presents a novel approach to identifying earthquake-related incidents from Twitter, leveraging a newly curated database of nearly 100,000 posts curated from the 2015 Gorkha event. The proposed model applies a multi-stage pipeline that combines keyword and entity-driven search strategies with natural language processing and image analysis. By capitalizing on social media's potential for disaster response and public engagement, the system effectively categorizes new tweets into relevant categories, facilitating more efficient support and information dissemination during crises.

A group $G$ possesses the property $R$ if every twisted conjugacy class under every automorphism of $G$ is finite. This property is strictly stronger than being of Radon type. In this work, we establish that the first radial group and the finitely generated pro-$p$ abelian group both satisfy the property $R$ when considering twisted conjugacy defined by their respective inner automorphisms.

We present a rapid and efficient algorithm for high-dimensional time-resolved spectroscopy and scattering data analysis. By modeling time-resolved changes as linear combinations of basis functions, the algorithm performs model-based principal component analysis followed by non-linear least-squares global fitting of time-gated principal component amplitudes. These parameters track time-varyuating cross-sections along a specific quantum pathway. By enforcing continuity constraints on the amplitude functions, the approach significantly reduces the number of independent fitted parameters, thereby increasing fitting stability. The method's robustness and efficiency in handling high-dimensional datasets were demonstrated through the analysis of time-resolved X-ray scattering data capturing the kinetics of photoexcited pyrene molecules in a polymer.

This study introduces the Self-Collection Naturalistic Driving Dataset (SceNDD), a comprehensive dataset gathered through a self-collected framework. It encompasses 100 hours of video footage captured from 11 vehicles equipped with a 360-degree camera system, featuring data derived from 30 real-world driving sessions. The dataset includes synchronized recordings of vehicle telemetry, GPS tracking, and acceleration metrics alongside corresponding visual inputs and their respective outputs. Furthermore, it offers preprocessed versions including keyframes, semantic segmentation, and object detection data. These resources aim to facilitate research and educational efforts in the fields of self-driving vehicles and intelligent transportation systems.

Within the framework of the bulk/boundary correspondence in boundary conformal field theory, we investigate entanglement wedge cross-section (EWCS) and its relationship with reflected entropy. Building upon recent advancements in defining quasi-universality for EWCS, this study defines a corresponding universal quantity for boundary CFT and examines its behavior under local perturbations. By leveraging the Ryu Takehashi formula alongside the Iwamiya-Jian-Wang-Zhang inequality, an area-law bound governing the reflected entropy of the entanglement wedge is established. Furthermore, the paper explores the emergence of a new class of geometry within boundary CFT through the generalized Riemann-Hilbert manifold (GRHM) and investigates the geometric structure of the reflected entropy via complex analysis techniques. These findings offer novel insights into the nature of reflected entropy and its underlying entanglement structure.

Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) offer a promising solution for enhancing wireless system performance. This paper investigates a scenario where RIS is integrated into orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) architectures. By applying beamforming techniques to the RIS, the authors demonstrate significant improvements in communication quality. Furthermore, they address the challenge of selecting optimal frequencies within the subcarrier region. A suboptimal algorithm is developed to minimize total frequency consumption across these subcarriers, and the authors derive an upper bound for the associated approximation error. In addition, the study examines the impact of imperfect channel estimation on system behavior. Numerical simulations confirm that the proposed methods effectively reduce the number of required subcarriers while maintaining robust performance even under conditions of imperfect channel knowledge.

The swift and widespread coronavirus pandemic has triggered extensive global health crises. While numerous nations have implemented non-essential business closures and travel bans to curb transmission, the virus continues to spread. As a highly contagious respiratory pathogen, SARS-CoV-2 primarily transmits through close human interaction. Consequently, identifying individuals with whom an infected person had close proximity within the last 14 days is crucial for preventing further cases. To address this, several countries have launched digital non-pharmaceutical interventions known as "contact tracing" apps. These applications utilize mobile technology to warn users of recent exposure to confirmed cases. However, these tools raise significant privacy concerns regarding the potential collection of sensitive user data, including geolocation history and social networks, which could be exploited for purposes beyond public health safety. Consequently, this study introduces a privacy-conscious, blockchain-based non-certificate contact tracing framework called "TraceBlock." This system leverages blockchain technology to create an immutable ledger that stores user data in a decentralized manner, ensuring transparency and eliminating reliance on a central authority. Furthermore, TraceBlock employs zero-knowledge cryptography to enable private key-based authentication and the secure, anonymous verification of infection status. Additionally, the system supports non-certificate tracing, allowing users to remain unverified while still facilitating the identification of close contacts. Finally, the paper evaluates the proposed framework's computational and communication overheads, as well as the privacy safeguards inherent to the design.

This study introduces a standard classical framework for analyzing how shared classical information produces observable correlations between outcomes measured on spatially separated systems. The analysis further examines the role of quantum entanglement in generating measurable outcome correlations. Additionally, a classical interpretation of local hidden variables is explored, highlighting the significance of the measurement context in explaining outcome correlations. These insights are corroborated through a standard Monte Carlo simulation of the 1D spin-1/2 Heisenberg model, which accurately reproduces the full quantum entanglement spectrum across varying temperatures. Finally, a classical explanation is provided for the conflict between quantum mechanics and the principles of locality, as formalized by Bell's theorem.

This work presents a code generator built in ACL2 tailored for abstract block structure, designed to produce concrete programs in Scheme and C from block-structure schemas. The tool implements both structural and value-based parameterization while ensuring formal verification of resulting concrete programs and their parameterized ancestors to guarantee correctness.

Astronomers have identified a group of asteroids in the outer main belt, designated as the Eros group, which is linked to the three-body resonance $3/1$. This group exhibits a radial width of approximately $0.06$ astronomical units (au) and a semi-major axis width of $0.04$ au. To investigate the origins of this structure, we conducted N-body simulations using an analytical potential to model the asteroid orbits. This approach included the gravitational influence of Jupiter and the $3/1$ mean motion resonance, along with the Yarkovsky effect. Our simulations demonstrated that the Eros group's formation is a cumulative outcome of orbital resonances and the gradual shift of the $3/1$ resonance caused by the asteroid's drift. These findings align with the observed distribution of the Eros group and the associated $2/1$ and $1/2$ resonances. Furthermore, our simulations indicate that the Eros group's current position is the result of a slow shift in the group's center over time, driven by the Yarkovsky effect. This process suggests that the group's location is currently at the leading edge of an asteroid family, which was originally created by a single parent body fragmentation event.
Building upon a renowned Ramanujan formula expressing odd zeta values, this paper introduces a novel identity of the same kind that incorporates the Hurwitz zeta function.

This article surveys recent machine learning applications to the algebraic geometry of classical moduli spaces. After briefly outlining ML fundamentals and the various ML-aided computational algebraic geometry techniques, the paper highlights emerging opportunities and challenges for employing these models within geometric representation learning.

This study examines the production of $J/\psi+\chi_{c0}$ via $e^+e^-$ annihilation at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=10.58$ GeV, utilizing data from the BEPCII detector. Angular distributions were analyzed in the laboratory frame, center-of-mass frame, and center-of-mass frame after boosting to the $\rho$-meson rest frame. The resulting data for the angular distribution parameters $a$, $b$, and $c$ for $J/\psi+\chi_{c0}$ production deviate significantly from experimental measurements, whereas predictions for $J/\psi+\chi_{c1}$ align well with existing data. Furthermore, theoretical calculations for the cross sections corresponding to the final states $J/\psi+\chi_{c0,1}$ exceed the observed experimental cross sections by a substantial margin.

This paper introduces a unique approach to managing signals within the context of privacy-preserving communication systems. It evaluates the security implications and operational efficiency of various PIN protocols applied to Signal's end-to-end encryption framework. By integrating anthropometric data with a rigorous security analysis, our findings reveal distinct patterns: a significant majority of users demonstrate robust adherence to current Signal PIN procedures. Conversely, enthusiastic users tend to reset their PINs frequently, whereas casual users adopt a hands-off attitude towards PIN updates. Furthermore, our analysis highlights a critical vulnerability wherein the current Signal PIN algorithm is susceptible to brute force attacks, potentially compromising the integrity of encrypted communication sessions. These results underscore the need for future research into more resilient PIN encryption schemes tailored to diverse user behaviors.

This paper proposes a novel approach to numerically integrate the direct solar irradiance equation over the Earth-central line-of-sight. The strategy involves restructuring the integral and applying Gaussian quadrature. This method achieves high precision with few calculation steps, making it especially valuable for time-intensive simulations such as solar resource assessment. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this quadrature formulation is equivalent to expressing solar irradiance as a specific weighted combination of squared Euclidean distances between the Sun and the point of integration on Earth. We also examine the method's performance during eclipses and the Sun's apparent diurnal motion.

Optimizing deep networks relies heavily on second-order information, particularly that of the Hessian, either in its entirety or via approximations like Generalized Gauss-Newton. While second-order methods often yield superior performance, their application is hindered by the prohibitive computational costs associated with storing the Hessian, especially in high-dimensional contexts. Consequently, researchers have developed various strategies to approximate the Hessian using random projections or sampling. However, existing full-batch approaches are limited to very large datasets, whereas stochastic variants fail with underparametrized networks. This paper introduces a novel, data-independent diagonal Hessian approximation designed for deep networks, which is theoretically grounded and empirically proven to closely match the full diagonal Hessian. Our approach is implemented efficiently using batch processing and can also be adapted for stochastic optimization. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a storage-efficient batch second-order method leveraging this approximation outperforms both standard second-order techniques and stochastic optimizers on extensive datasets, bridging the previous gap between methodologies.

This study examines the extent to which inanimate noun gender is encoded in contemporary word embeddings, aiming to assess both the efficacy of existing Grammatical Gender (GG) prediction models and the degree of gender bias in these representations. We introduce a novel, gender-neutralizing projection that significantly improves prediction accuracy across three tested Pseudo-Curminized (PCM) variants. Additionally, we established a robust PCM-variant specific GG prediction framework. Our experiments, conducted on three major embedding types, demonstrate that while the method works, the signals remain weak; the strongest correlations appear only in models trained on gendered data, and even these fail to capture the nuance of the three-way gender distinctions found in source texts like Wikipedia and DeWikipedia.

This work explores the relationship between stiffness and the dynamical properties of stationary probability measures $\mu$ within the context of the random Schur algorithm. Specifically, we demonstrate that for the dynamical pair $(\mathcal{X},\mu)$, three properties are equivalent: (i) $\mu$ is not weakly mixing, (ii) $(\mathcal{X},\mu)$ is not generated, and (iii) $(\mathcal{X},\mu)$ is not stiff. Additionally, we prove that a stationary measure $\mu$ is stiff if and only if its support $\Omega_{\mu}$ is contained within the closure of the set of periodic points of $\mu$ under the shift map induced by $(\mathcal{A},\mu)$.

Although generalization to novel categories is crucial for practical object detection and pose estimation, current methods often fail to handle unseen classes effectively. While zero-shot detection has seen recent success, pose estimation remains underexplored in this area. This study introduces a straightforward yet powerful method for achieving zero-shot 3D human pose estimation. We adapt an existing zero-shot detector to generate dense 2D landmark maps for unseen categories and sample corresponding 3D poses from the prior using these maps. We demonstrate that simple strategies like this achieve state-of-the-art results on the challenging MPI-INF-3DHP zero-shot test set. Furthermore, we prove that high-quality zero-shot estimation is attainable even without any class-specific training data.

However, accurate forecasting remains a challenging endeavor due to the complex dynamics of road networks. This paper introduces a novel approach to causal inference, beginning with the construction of a Structural Causal Model (SCM) that represents causal mechanisms as probabilistic differential equations. The approach's first stage involves inferring the immediate cause-and-effect relationships from data using a variation of the PC algorithm. Subsequently, causal effects are derived by integrating knowledge of these immediate links with the identified model of causal mechanisms. To facilitate flexible modeling of causal mechanisms, the method employs a hierarchical Gaussian process to approximate probability density functions. To validate this approach, numerical experiments are conducted on both synthetic datasets and a real-world benchmark consisting of the "Simpson's Paradox" dataset.

The advent of advanced radio interferometers, such as the Very Large Array and the Low-Frequency Array, has significantly expanded our observational capabilities, enabling detailed studies of diverse phenomena including solar flares, galactic nuclei, and the Milky Way's diffuse emission. Building on this progress, our group has developed a Python package named `spectrum` to facilitate data reduction for the Low-Frequency Array. This tool streamlines tasks like antenna-based calibration, beam modeling, source fitting, and uncertainty estimation. We detail the package's architecture and demonstrate its utility through two practical examples: determining sources of radio frequency interference and isolating components within a galaxy.

The film industry is a highly dynamic sector characterized by significant financial stakes, where distributors and exhibitors face critical challenges in accurately forecasting an film's revenue to maximize returns. This study addresses these challenges by building a predictive model to estimate box office earnings. By utilizing a dataset of 1,041 movies, the research analyzes the relationships between various attributes—such as marketing budget, release date, and cast/crew star power—and corresponding revenues. The findings confirm that these attributes serve as meaningful predictors for sales. Furthermore, the work demonstrates that employing the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network architecture yields a robust, high-accuracy model for this revenue forecasting task.

The contemporary electrical power grid is a vast, interconnected system designed to sustain specific frequency levels and voltage profiles. Deviations from these targets can result in power disruptions, blackouts, or system instability. This paper introduces a frequency and voltage control strategy that leverages the interaction between battery energy storage systems (BESS) and inverter-based resources (IBRs). Specifically, it examines how these batteries can be integrated into IBRs to enhance frequency regulation, while simultaneously ensuring voltage stability. By analyzing how BEES contribute to the overall frequency response of an IBR system, this research offers a practical approach to improving grid performance. Experimental results demonstrate that this control strategy effectively addresses frequency fluctuations and maintains voltage stability across various operational conditions.

The automotive ecosystem is a complex, collaborative network of stakeholders, systems, and components designed to deliver sophisticated, emergent functionalities such as in-entertainment systems, driver assistance tools, and driver fatigue monitoring. However, managing these intricate collections of interdependent systems and components presents significant hurdles. This study introduces a system-to-system methodology tailored to address these complexities, leveraging systems engineering and design science principles. The proposed approach is validated through a pilot application within the pilot scenario of an automotive infotainment system, with a resulting framework presented in an accompanying system of systems framework.

We report the detection of a spectral feature in the OJ 287 blazar that is consistent with Fe K$\alpha$ emission. This observation occurred during a major outburst in 2019, which also produced an ultraviolet and soft X-ray excess. This surplus flux is likely caused by the relativistic jet impacting the primary accretion disc, a process that generated a transient X-ray flare from the disc surface. This flare was intense enough to create a relativistic, Doppler-boosted Fe K$\alpha$ emission line. This event marks the first time Fe K$\alpha$ has been identified in an active disc associated with an active galactic nucleus.

This study examines the stability of local minima and other stable local points within real landscapes derived from their associated dynamical systems in complex spaces. We demonstrate that, apart from rare exceptions, every stable local point is located at a Stokes line, with the vast majority of these being Stokes points. Additionally, we show that most Stokes points are stable local maxima.

This paper investigates the discrimination of non-orthogonal two-state systems in quantum systems across multiple scenarios, contrasting online and offline strategies. Specifically, we demonstrate that employing online methods can achieve a higher average success probability for identifying pure states compared to offline approaches. Additionally, when states are mixed, an offline method remains optimal under certain conditions; this includes maintaining constant results regardless of the number of copies available.

Baryon production is analyzed within the QCD string fragmentation framework. Within this model, breakups serve as the fundamental mechanism for forming baryons. The study investigates the impact of varying string breakups and their associated parameters on baryon multiplicity ratios and spin structures. Distinct differences are observed between octet and decuplet baryons, as well as within specific decuplet components such as the $\Delta^{++}$ and $\Omega^{-}$. Furthermore, the orientation of baryon spins is found to be sensitive to the quantum properties of string endpoints, which represent quarks and diquarks. Theoretical predictions for baryon multiplicity and spin, which address gaps in current experimental data, are presented for LHCb and RHIC operations.

We investigate the impact of localized plasma inflows within solar active regions on helioseismic travel times, aiming to explain variations in these measurements observed throughout the solar cycle. Utilizing data from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) on the Solar Dynamics Observatory, we identified and modeled flows in active regions, subsequently calculating their effect on inward travel times via a two-dimensional ray theory model. These predicted perturbations were contrasted with actual HMI-derived travel time anomalies. The results indicate that flow-induced disturbances account for approximately 80% of the travel time deviations associated with active regions, demonstrating that local inflows are the primary driver of these seismic anomalies. Furthermore, this influence correlates with variations in active region size, magnetic flux, and inflow velocity, collectively explaining roughly 80% of travel time changes in regions where flows occur. These findings support the conclusion that active region inflows play a crucial role in interpreting helioseismic travel time data across the solar cycle.

Light field technology has garnered significant attention for its potential to achieve high-resolution results through computational merging of multiple low-dose exposures. While this approach offers flexibility in hardware requirements, existing methods often introduce severe artifacts such as noise, blurring, or saturated regions when combining these images. To address these issues, we propose a new technique that leverages the intrinsic relationships within chained views to generate merged high-resolution images more effectively. Our method begins by classifying every sub-aperture image as either usable or unusable based on its local structural quality. For the retained images, we apply a chained-view strategy to select the optimal sub-aperture for each spatial position, thereby minimizing artifacts. Finally, a deep learning model is employed to perform joint spatial and tone-mapping to deliver superior image quality. Experimental results indicate that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, as demonstrated by both higher quantitative metrics and improved visual outcomes.

The two dominant paradigms for vector-based cross-lingual information retrieval are contrastive learning and contrastive vs. non-contrastrative pair ranking. This paper conducts an extensive empirical study comparing the effectiveness of these two approaches in a cross-lingual zero-shot setting using vector search. We evaluate models trained on CoCOA 2018 and COCORIA datasets across 25 language pairs, testing 25 different search configurations for each training method. The results indicate that contrastive learning models consistently outperform fine-tired embedding retrieval, even when fine-tired embeddings are adapted using vectorized query rephrase. Furthermore, fine-tired embeddings demonstrate greater robustness across diverse languages compared. Finally, incorporating query rephrase with fine-tired embeddings yields stronger performance than applying rephrase to standard contrastive learning models. We conclude that hybrid methods combining rephrase and fine-tired embeddings surpass both fine-tired and rephrase-only approaches in cross-lingual dense retrieval.

The rapidly expanding domain of public health policy relies on census and survey data to generate estimates regarding population characteristics, a process that varies in representativeness based on whether units are drawn randomly or treated equally. This study introduces a unified Bayesian framework for classification tasks, such as determining demographic status, that explicitly addresses varying levels of sample representability. By incorporating document content alongside external knowledge of the interview context, this approach mitigates biases inherent in non-random sampling strategies found in most public health research. Consequently, it offers statistically rigorous methods to produce policy-critical estimates from datasets with unequal representation, a significant advancement for the field.

This paper introduces a novel framework for quantum betting that incorporates quantum static work, utilizing the measure of ergotropy to represent the betting "capital" invested. By defining quantum bets as the specification of conditional state preparations triggered by the outcome of a contest "opponent," we establish quantum betting "profits" through the difference between the resulting state and the one prepared otherwise. To formalize this approach, we introduce an associated "utility" quantified using the quantum relative entropy. Our findings demonstrate that the combined use of utility and profit serves as an effective apparatus for dissecting the fundamental mechanics of the contest "opponent."

This study introduces a novel analytical framework designed to examine the radial density distribution of matter within a protoplanetary disk during formation. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on numerous free parameters and complex numerical simulations, our model is parameter-free and derived from fundamental physical principles. The analysis demonstrates that the mass flux originating from the inner regions toward the outer edges results in a distribution characterized by a significant concentration of matter closest to the central star. Furthermore, our results indicate that this structural feature remains robust even in the presence of non-axisymmetric spiral arms.

To facilitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors (ADCs) in astrometry, we have developed a new simulation tool that models the differential atmospheric dispersion (ADM) and the associated effects of an ADC. This software was validated using both theoretical models and data from the ESO Paranal Observatory, and it offers a customizable code module for users to integrate specific ADC characteristics. Additionally, the tool provides a utility to compute optimal observation times by minimizing the magnitude of ADM and ADC-induced effects. We also present sample astrometric estimates of both ADM and the residual error after correction, derived from simulations for the European Southern Observatory (ESO) and Las Cumbres Observatory Global Network (LCCT).

This study introduces a hierarchical latent variable model designed to capture complex multi-period patterns in multi-dimensional time series. By employing multiple recurrent neural networks (RNNs) as latent variable generators, the framework facilitates the joint learning of multiple nested latent variables, which are subsequently utilized to simulate the entire series. Through the maximization of the likelihood function, the approach models the statistical dependencies among these learned latent variables. The resulting learned models are capable of capturing both long-term and short-term dynamics in high-dimensional temporal data. Furthermore, the method supports probabilistic forecasting by providing prediction intervals for future values and can be extended to learn representations within a semi-supervised setting.

The rapid advancement of deep learning has generated significant ethical issues, particularly concerning data privacy and algorithmic bias. While existing research addresses these challenges by employing differential privacy and fairness optimization, such approaches often overlook the uncertainty inherent in both the model and the data. To address this gap, this study introduces a unified framework that simultaneously mitigates bias and safeguards privacy while quantifying uncertainty. Specifically, the model incorporates three distinct uncertainty metrics: data uncertainty within the input, uncertainty regarding the decision outcome, and uncertainty about an individual's group membership. Our approach utilizes variational inference to learn a latent representation space where embeddings are generated as probabilistic distributions, thereby capturing both algorithmic and data-driven uncertainty alongside enhanced privacy protections and reduced bias. Empirical evaluations on three benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

We introduce a supersymmetric dark matter model featuring a TeV-scale right-handed neutrino, which fits current experimental data. Unlike the minimal supersymmetric standard model, this right-handed neutradoes not acquire Majorana mass at tree level but instead gains it via a Yukawa coupling with a right-handed isosinglet superfield, denoted as $S$. We investigate a scenario where $S$ functions as a dark matter candidate, while the right-handed neutradoes, acting as a fermion, serves as its superpartner. This construction allows $S$ to be the weak gauge singlin, making it a viable dark matter candidate within the supersymmetric framework. We further explore the phenomenology of this model, particularly the implications for collider searches at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) and direct detection experiments. We find that the phenomenology of this model is distinct from that of the minimal supersymmetric standard model due to the presence of the right-handed neutradoes, which can lead to new signatures at the LHC and direct detection experiments. We also discuss the implications of this model for direct detection experiments, particularly the Xenon1T experiment, which has recently placed stringent constraints on the right-handed isosinglet superfield $S$. We find that the phenomenology of this model is consistent with the direct constraints imposed by the Xenon1T experiment, particularly in the region where the right-handed isosinglet superfield $S$ has a mass of a few hundred GeV.

This study examines a wireless powered communication network featuring an external energy harvester and an intelligent reflecting surface (IRS). The base station (BS) transmits energy signals, enabling user terminals (UTs) to harvest power for data transmission. The primary objective is to maximize network throughput by jointly optimizing the BS's power allocation and the passive beamforming strategies employed at the IRS. To address this, two efficient algorithms are proposed: one is a block coordinate descent (BCD) method that decomposes the original optimization problem into two simpler sub-problems for sequential resolution, and the other is a novel joint optimization framework based on conic programming reformulation and fractional programming techniques for throughput maximization. Simulation results demonstrate the high efficiency of the proposed solutions in achieving significant performance gains.

This work introduces a newly developed framework for determining the distribution of Gamow-Teller strength, which operates independently of nuclear models and relies solely on experimental data. The method's validity is validated by a precise analysis of $^{133}\text{Ba}$ decay, during which calculated inter-nucleon interactions align exceptionally well with established values. The strength distribution derived through this approach is then utilized to perform nuclear structure calculations for $^{133}\text{Ba}$, yielding results that achieve quantitative agreement with known single-particle energies. The calculated $\beta^-$-decay rates also demonstrate quantitative consistency with experimental measurements. Finally, the proposed formalism is applied to predict the distribution of Gamow-Teller strength in $^{135}\text{Xe}$ decay; the resulting predictions align well with existing experimental constraints.

We analyze a framework incorporating both standard and right-handed neutrinos alongside a scalar triplet, allowing us to examine lepton number violation driven by this new representation. By leveraging the extensive lepton number mixing induced by the scalar triplet, we demonstrate that the final baryon asymmetry from the charged scalar's decays is consistently determined by its CP asymmetry in those decays, regardless of whether the scalar is on-shell, and without relying on thermal out-of-equilibrium conditions. This finding holds true in scenarios where both scalar and neutral right-handed neutrains are on-shell, as well as in cases involving their respective thermal equilibrium. This robustness persists even if dark matter is constituted by right-handed neutrains, notably in the presence of the sterile dark sector scalar triplet. In such configurations, we show that the neutrino mass matrix element $m_{11}$ and the baryon asymmetry share identical thermal limits, meaning a vanishing $m_{11}$ arises whenever dark matter comprises right-handed neutrains within this model class.

This study addresses the challenge of controlling unknown dynamical systems, specifically those characterized by stable dynamics with a significant transient phase, when only a solitary trial is permitted. While previous approaches relying solely system measurements have yielded only suboptimal performance, we introduce a new method that utilizes accessible side information, such as the theoretical ideal trajectory, to achieve substantially better results. Our approach involves designing a specialized measurement strategy to gather crucial data from the side information prior to executing actual control, thereby optimizing subsequent decision-making. We formalize this process as a Sequential Design and Control (SDC) framework and analyze its behavior using large deviation theory to ensure design efficiency. We also provide a rigorous mathematical proof demonstrating that our proposed control algorithm is asymptotically optimal with high probability. The validity of our method is illustrated through simulations of experimental tasks involving a double pendulum system stabilized by an inverted pendulum, where the side information is represented as the feasible motion manifold.

This review summarizes the authors' prior publications, establishing the conformal field theory (CTCF) framework for Toda theories and elucidating the role of flag manifold geometry within it. The discussion highlights key features of these models, including their symmetries, dualities, and the physical significance of bigraphical calculus in field operator construction. By synthesizing field operator calculus, Toda conformal field theory is recast using bigraphical methods, with the field operators defined as specific operator kernels acting on sections of line bundles over the flag manifold. The study further explores the chiral algebra, which is shown to correspond to the representation of Clifford blocks within calculus, and demonstrates how the W-algebra corresponds to specific subgraphical structures. The report concludes by linking the W-algebra to the Calogero-Moser spectral problem, identifying a topological correspondence between the conformal field theory and the Calogero-Moser map.

Generative adversarial networks (GANs) have established themselves as premier tools for learning complex data distributions, yet they present significant training challenges, particularly when scaling to high resolutions. This study introduces a novel, memory-efficient architecture designed to mitigate the prohibitive computational costs often associated with GANs. By restructuring the generator and discriminator into parallel subnetworks that process spatial dimensions independently, our approach leverages the factical symmetry of the image grid. This method effectively reuses weights across these dimensions, substantially shrinking the total parameter count of the model. Experiments conducted on diverse benchmarks—including real and synthetic image datasets—demonstrate that the proposed system attains comparable performance to full-sized models while utilizing only a fraction of the required memory.

A field test of a quantum key distribution (KDK) system was conducted in the Yangtze River, utilizing two boats positioned 52 kilometers apart. This 42-hour transmission run operated without phase locking between the vessels. The study confirms an extended transmission distance achieved without requiring phase synchronization and establishes a foundation for future quantum communication along riverways and other arteries.

This paper examines Toeplitz algebras formed from every closed, translation-invariant subspace of bounded uniformly continuous functions defined on complex types $X$ within the framework of Euclidean types $ \mathbb{C}^{n} $. An analysis is provided for the quotient and intersection behaviors associated with these algebras. When the order of type $X$ equals the full dimension $n$, there exists a description of the quotient algebra relative to its maximal ideal and an identification of its other components.

Although object detection has achieved impressive results on well-known benchmarks, existing methods typically rely on manually labeling specific categories, limiting their utility in real-world scenarios. This paper introduces a novel object detection approach capable of identifying unseen categories without any labeled training data. Our method is motivated by the observation that objects across different categories often share underlying structural patterns. By leveraging shared representations through a common backbone, the framework transfers categorical information to recognize previously unknown classes. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that the approach achieves strong results, even in zero-shot configurations. Furthermore, the proposed technique performs effectively in few-shot and general zero-shot settings, establishing new state-of-the-art benchmarks.

We introduce a novel, highly efficient PDR modeling code that solves the key physical equations—energy balance, radiative transfer, and ionization chemistry—in up to 3D space. This approach utilizes a non-uniform adaptive mesh based on the specific requirements of each equation, which is dynamically refined or coarsened to ensure necessary resolution while maintaining performance on large scales. Additionally, the system employs a pre-computed chemical network lookup table to further accelerate calculations. As an illustration, we apply the 3D variant of this 3D PDR model to a complex scenario within the Carina Nebula, specifically modeling the interaction between stellar winds and radiation from massive stars with CARMA and ALMA data. The simulation successfully reproduces the observed CO(2-1) emission and the fine-structure line profiles of sulfur ([S III]) and oxygen ([O III]).

Transformer models have achieved remarkable success across numerous tasks, yet the core principles behind this success remain unclear. Existing literature highlights various aspects of the architecture, but these insights are often fragmented and lack a unified framework for practical application. This work synthesizes fundamental concepts—attention stability, attention information density, transformer convergence, and the relationship between Transformer and self-revealing Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs)—to provide a unified perspective for understanding and employing these architectures. The authors first detail how fixed-transformations attention ensures estimation stability, then link attention mechanisms to RNNs to derive the theoretical conditions for Transformer convergence. Furthermore, the work proposes a novel metric for measuring attention sparsity and demonstrates its utility across multiple tasks. Finally, a comprehensive review of recent research is presented, categorized according to these fundamental concepts to highlight directions for future investigation.

This study introduces a flexible parametric proportional hazards framework designed to model multiple cause-of-death statistics across varying time periods. It features a smooth parameterization for time-varying cause-specific mortality hazards, a cause-specific Cox model with cause-specific hazards, and incorporates an indicator variable for a temporal dummy to capture shifts in mortality patterns. By employing B-spline transformations, the model enables flexible estimation of cause of death changes. It supports the estimation of standardized cause of death rates while maintaining a unified modeling structure. The proposed methodology is validated using simulated data and further illustrated through application to national mortality data from the United States, United Kingdom, and China.

To reduce inference costs, a common strategy involves sharing neural network architectures across multiple tasks. However, when performing neural architecture search (NAS), this sharing can lead to detrimental interference among the resulting models on common substructures, often degrading overall performance. This study investigates how to optimize architectures to minimize such interference. We demonstrate that the frequency of operator disagreement between paired models serves as a reliable predictor of interference levels; specifically, higher disagreement correlates with stronger interference. Leveraging this relationship, we introduce an architecture search task that explicitly optimizes for reduced interference by defining an original interference metric and integrating it into a novel, interference-aware NAS framework through constraint optimization. Experimental results across a diverse set of tasks reveal that our approach achieves significantly lower interference compared to standard methods, yielding improvements of up to 10% in task accuracy.

Time series analysis has become increasingly vital across many fields, particularly in the era of Big Data. A key step in analyzing these data sets is the extraction of summary statistics or features, which are essential for both time series regression and classification. However, existing methods are often limited to handling just a single feature at a time. This study introduces a new, flexible framework for generating concurrent multiple features from time series. Notably, this framework is model-agnostic and can integrate with any existing method, regardless of its complexity. We evaluate the performance of this proposed approach using both synthetic data and real-world datasets within the context of time series regression. The results demonstrate that this versatile design effectively streamlines the feature generation process.

We specify tangible and minimal conditions ensuring that a proper geodesically complete CAT(0) space possesses a stable fundamental group at all large finite quotients. We also explore connections between these properties and the asymptotic geometry of the space. As a application, we demonstrate that for a connected reductive algebraic group $\mathbf G$ defined over $\mathbb R$, any quotient $\mathbf G(\mathbb R)/\Gamma$ has a stable (and thus vice-morse) first Chattersley class at all sufficiently large finite quotients, where $\Gamma$ is a lattice.

Translation Quality Assessment (TQA) involves evaluating the proficiency of a translator who renders content from a source language into a target language. This study examines the consistency and dependability of TQA when performed by both machine and human experts. Our findings indicate that while the high quality of contemporary machine translation (MT) makes it difficult to discern between human and automated outputs, TQA reliability is compromised by low inter-annotator agreement. We propose a consensus-based TQA strategy that yields significantly better performance. Additionally, our results demonstrate that both the consensus-based method and standard TQA achieve superior outcomes when the evaluation is conducted by a group of annotators rather than an individual.

This study introduces a deposition matrix designed to achieve a uniform distribution of particles within random-scattering systems. We examine various two-dimensional geometries, specifically utilizing arrays of metallic and dielectric rods. Results indicate that the deposition matrix outperforms conventional methods, such as state-of-the-art deposition algorithms. Furthermore, this work provides a theoretical framework explaining how the matrix achieves precise particle distribution.

Pruning techniques have demonstrated significant potential for enhancing the computational efficiency of deep neural networks by reducing the volume of parameters. However, existing pruning methodologies often fail to address the inherent non-convexity of the underlying optimization problems, which restricts their ability to achieve optimal compression rates. This paper introduces a novel global pruning approach that leverages recent advancements in convex optimization. Our method systematically prunes individual weights across fully connected layers and subsequently analyzes the architecture of the resulting sub-networks. The structural analysis reveals characteristic patterns in these pruned networks, insights which serve as the basis for a new class of learning-driven pruning techniques. Experimental evaluations across various image classification benchmarks confirm that our global pruning algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art competitive methods in compression efficiency while maintaining comparable accuracy.

This paper examines the expected value of a lottery ticket in the context of owning $N$ such tickets, with applications to the "multiplication" or multiplier add-on. We establish that as the number of drawn winning numbers and the probability of having multiple winning tickets increase, individually and collectively, the ticket's expected value drops. This decline is attributed to a lower average share of the jackpot when more people win simultaneously. Consequently, the average return per ticket is lower when multiple winners occur compared to the scenario where only a single player wins. Furthermore, provided the probability of a tie (multiple winners) is sufficiently small, having between one and ten tickets remains the optimal strategy to maximize the average expected return. The authors demonstrate that the standard single-tie assumption is insufficient for accurately estimating the expected return of typical lotteries, such as the UK National Lottery, and the UK Lotto.

This study determines the anomalous dimensions governing single and doubly light operator twists up to six-loop order, which are essential inputs for next-generation analyses of two-hadron light-cone sum rules. The computation was performed at both large and numerical small values of the perturbation parameter. Notably, the work incorporates contributions from highly complex operators involving five or more legs. Furthermore, several results are presented in forms that are compact and suitable for computational implementation.

We present a theoretical study of valley Hall response influenced by Dirac cone curvature, demonstrating that applying static strain can generate a non-zero valley Hall response in three specific two-dimensional materials: graphone, graphene, and twisted bilayer graphene. The analysis indicates that static pressure, another form of static strain, generates the valley Hall response exclusively in graphone among the materials examined here. The anisotropic character of the valley Hall response in both graphone and graphene stems directly from the curvature of their Dirac cones. The anisotropic valley Hall response in twisted bilayer graphene is attributed to an interference between interstational Dirac cone curvature and intristational Dirac cone curvature. These findings are expected to facilitate the creation of novel valley electron devices.

For the inaugural time, this study tackles an understudied challenge: performing unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) for semantic segmentation in image regions. While previous UAD approaches for standard tasks have largely relied on image-level labels, extending these concepts to segmentations remains difficult because the available data consists solely of segmentations without bounding labels. To address this, we introduce a novel framework that adapts pre-trained classification models to perform segmentation via domain adaptation. The approach utilizes a newly developed region encoder to extract features for each area and a domain adaptation classifier to generate labels for these regions. In a pioneering step, we apply self-supervised learning with pseudo-labels specifically to area-based labels. The resulting model is capable of performing segmentation without requiring any labeled images from the target domain. The effectiveness of this region-focused adaptation strategy is validated across two datasets: the cross-domain transition from the Cityscape to the ADE20K dataset, as well as a challenging adaptation between data from two different cameras within the ADE20K set.

t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) is a widely utilized algorithm for visualizing high-dimensional datasets by leveraging an initial deep learning model. It achieves this through the calculation of local similarity distributions using a Gaussian kernel for input space and a standard Euclidean distance metric for the embedded space. This study introduces a new approach to enhancing both the quality and interpretability of t-SNE visualizations. We propose a Bayesian framework that simultaneously optimizes the kernel parameters of the input space and the low-dimensional embedding. By employing a hierarchical Bayesian model, the joint inference of the deep network architecture and embedding space is performed. Specifically, the revised methodology utilizes a locally adaptive Student's $t$-distribution, extending the original t-SNE approach. This innovative distribution allows for more precise modeling of proximity within diverse data regimes and facilitates the integration of uncertainty regarding both the embedding and kernel parameters into the objective function.

This research investigates the low-energy landscape of the two-dimensional Fermi polaron system, specifically focusing on scenarios involving population imbalance. Employing a machine-learning-driven variational method grounded in tensor networks, the study examines both homogeneous and impurity-paired states across the full spectrum of interaction strengths—from contact interactions mediated by two-body bound states to unitary and BEC regimes in various regimes. The primary finding is a ground state crossover, contingent on the ratio of the two populations, that shifts continuously from a polaron existing in the Fermi sea to molecular formation in the BEC limit. Additionally, the energy of the polaran deep within the BEC regime is calculated, demonstrating that the polaran ground state energy approaches zero as the coupling $g$ follows the asymptotic scaling $g \propto \ln(1/\delta n)$, with $\delta n$ denoting the population difference. Finally, the study identifies the precise boundary in the effective BCS-BEC crossover separating the ground state of free fermions (polarons) from bound pairs (molecules).

This paper investigates the analog and digital analog hybrid implementation, utilizing the framework of digital-analog quantum computing, for simulating spatially dispersed fermionic systems with spinless characteristics through various two-qubit gate types. Our findings demonstrate that for the efficient simulation of such systems, a linear qubit architecture is optimal over higher-dimensional connectivities. In a digital analog scheme leveraging spinless fermion interactions, domain wall representations facilitate near-optimal energy spectrum approximations achieved with approximately 1.6-fold qubit overprovisioning. While this approach can suffer from extensive phase accumulation, its impact is mitigated by incorporating Hadamard tests to determine interaction strengths adaptively.

This paper addresses the count of k-colorable graph substructures within an arbitrary host graph G, achievable by evaluating the substructure (or Tutte) polynomial of G at specific coordinates. While evaluating these polynomials is known to be #P-hard even on restricted graph classes, we introduce a novel approach for the number of such colorable subgraphs using a graph polynomial analogous to the chromatic polynomial. This new polynomial, evaluated at -1, precisely yields the count of k-colorable substructures. Furthermore, we demonstrate that generating polynomials of this type is itself a #P-hard task across even broadly limited graph families.
This work investigates the Hitchin connection defined over the compactification of the Teichmüller bundle, specifically for an algebraically compact one-dimensional curve genus $g \geq 2$.

The shift to remote work has become a permanent fixture in the business landscape, fundamentally altering the office environment and evolving employee psychological needs. This shift introduces unique challenges to mental well-being, particularly for managers who must navigate these shifts and mitigate the accompanying negative emotions. This study examines how Self-Determination Theory (SDT) can inform the support of psychological well-being among telecommuting staff. The research explores the emotional impacts of remote working and the strategies required to counteract them. By analyzing existing literature, the authors propose SDT as a robust framework for addressing the emotional challenges inherent to a remoter working lifestyle. Furthermore, the study highlights the necessity of SDT-based interventions to foster well-being and productivity, while also exploring the practical implementation of this theory in real-world work settings.

Using the ALICE detector at the LHC, this study investigates the elliptic flow, $v_2$, of electrons originating from beauty hadron decays, measured in Pb–Pb collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=5.02$ TeV. The analysis covers pseudorapidity ranges of $-2.5 < \eta < 2.5$ and transverse momentum intervals of $0.5 < p_{\rm T} < 15$ GeV/$c$, with the data compared to predictions from beauty particle models. The observed $v_2$ values are consistent with model predictions that attribute beauty quarks to source from cold nuclear matter prior to the collision and treat their interaction within the hot, dense medium as part of a beauty–charm–strange coalescence framework. The study further examines the dependence of $v_2$ on particle mass, finding it aligns with a pattern similar to that of strangeness. Additionally, transverse momentum dependence of $v_2$ is analyzed across varying centrality classes, with results compared to earlier LHCb measurements of $v_2$ for beauty hadrons themselves.

This paper explores various configurations of chromatic sets in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) for dimensions \(d \geq 2\). We establish both positive and negative findings concerning the existence of specific geometric structures, demonstrated through applications of the classical results of Szemerédi and Ruzsa. Additionally, utilizing techniques from harmonic analysis, the study derives findings regarding the distribution of distinct colors within finite collections of points.

This paper investigates the performance of optimal power control (OPC) in networks featuring a limited number of users, addressing a gap left by existing systems that focus primarily on large-user scenarios. We introduce a network-wide user count metric and establish an explicit upper bound for the extremal gain of OPC, which is governed by this limited user metric. Our findings indicate that the gain can become significantly large when our user count metric remains small, even as total user quantity increases. We also examine how this metric scales in dense networks, demonstrating that its magnitude is intrinsically tied to the distribution of active users. Consequently, this work broadens the scope of the square-root law, which characterizes optimal power control benefits in massive network contexts.

Categorization is a critical component of auditing workflows, such as classifying transactions into non-financial categories. While machine learning offers superior accuracy compared to non-explainable methods like rule-based systems, it acts as a "black box," obscuring the rationale behind predictions. This lack of transparency hinders its adoption in auditing contexts, where stakeholders must understand the logic driving outcomes. This study introduces and evaluates a new approach to explainable categorization that leverages the synergy between decision trees and natural language processing. Our methodology generates a natural language explanation for each transaction by combining its decision tree path with the semantic descriptions derived from support items. Experiments demonstrate that this method achieves higher explainability than black-box models without compromising accuracy. Furthermore, it significantly improves the efficiency of human auditors in a review setting by reducing both the time required to evaluate predictions and the frequency of errors.

The STrauss process is a point process defined by a specific density function, representing the number of point pairs within a given threshold distance. While its stationary and Palm distributions are fully characterized, its Ripley's $K$-function remains undefined. Consequently, its second-order properties, particularly those described by the structure function, cannot be explicitly formulated. This work demonstrates that the stationary STrauss process can be represented through a new thinning mechanism applied to a Poisson point process. This perspective allows for the derivation of its $K$-function and a theoretical framework for constructing random variables simulating the process. Furthermore, the study includes a validation of this construction method via a new simulation algorithm and an analysis of convergence rates based on large deviation principles.

The Generalized Uncertainty Principle (GUP) introduces a basic length scale, prompting a reassessment of the Schwarzschild metric in black hole physics. This re-evaluation leads to defining a GUP-inspired metric that modifies spacetime geometry near mass concentrations. By applying the tunneling method to derive emission rates for accretion disks, we observe that the characteristic fundamental length resulting from the GUP significantly influences the rates. Additionally, we demonstrate that the standard Schwarzschild radius emerges as a limiting case when the fundamental length approaches zero. Furthermore, we show that black hole evaporation rates remain finite rather than diverging at the inner horizon. Finally, we conclude that black holes do not completely vanish, suggesting a mechanism for their preservation.

This study addresses multitasking scheduling for real-time systems where central processors and remote edge nodes share the computational workload. The objective is to assign both tasks and their specific execution locations to minimize total completion time (makespan), subject to the constraint that each task must meet its real-time deadlines. The mathematical model incorporates the varying processing requirements for tasks, the overhead of switching locations, and the impact of task density on execution speed. The resulting formulation is classified as an NP-hard integer linear program. To address this complex problem, the authors introduce a heuristic algorithm designed to generate near-optimal solutions in polynomial time. The effectiveness of the proposed approach was validated through numerical experiments, which were also used to assess the model's performance.

Locomotion involving legs on deformable ground is difficult because the resulting complex dynamics are hard to model, control, and analyze. This study introduces the first rigorous mathematical framework for analyzing the gait cycles of legged robots traversing deformable terrain. The research establishes the necessary and sufficient stability and convergence conditions for these gaits. Theoretically, the approach is validated using the bipedal robot's rolling gait on granular media, specifically to demonstrate the convergence of step duration toward a constant value.

Internet of Things (IoT) networks are frequently deployed in expansive outdoor settings, such as farms and industrial zones, where reliable service is essential. To guarantee Quality-of-Service (QoS), network operators deploy specialized equipment and dedicated radio access nodes. However, when updating these networks with a new firmware release, there is a significant risk of introducing bugs that could disrupt service. Consequently, operators require methods to measure key performance indicators (KPIs) before and after these firmware rolls to ensure service quality. This study presents a framework designed to assess outdoor IoT network KPIs, specifically demonstrating its application in a rural scenario where an operator rolled out new firmware on their rural radio units. The framework utilizes crowdsourced IoT devices to gather metrics including packet loss ratio, latency, and received signal strength indicator (RSSI). It employs a data aggregation approach that combines the packet loss ratio and RSSI metrics to enhance the reliability of data collection. Furthermore, the research introduces a novel framework for calculating the packet loss ratio that relies on a two-way communication handshake. The study concludes by validating the proposed approach through real-world experiments conducted on a rural network infrastructure.

This investigation explores many-body localization within the framework of nonlinear $\sigma$-models, specifically addressing local Fock space self-energies across random second-neighbor Hubbard models on bipartite lattices. We observe that the imaginary component of the self-energy, denoted as $\mathrm{Im}\Sigma$, correlates with the decay rate of an initially localized state, thereby serving as a quantifiable indicator of localization. By analyzing systems with random single-particle hopping, we confirm that $\mathrm{Im}\Sigma$ aligns with exact numerical simulations in the strong disorder regime. Furthermore, utilizing a self-consistent scalar field approximation, we have mapped out the local mobility edges for random hopping interactions. In the strong disorder limit, our calculated mobility edges demonstrate remarkable agreement with precise numerical data.

Interactive graph search serves as a fundamental model for search problems in artificial intelligence, where a system queries a hidden shape via numerical responses. While prior research has explored this domain, this paper introduces kBM-IGS, a novel challenge within this framework. In kBM-Is, the objective is to determine if a hidden set of $k$ distinct target components exists and locate their intersection boundaries. The allowed operations involve unbounded boundary interval queries, which return the full set of shapes sharing the same boundary interval, and unbounded point queries, which identify the single target component containing a specific selected point. The authors demonstrate that for any query count $t$, there exists an algorithmic solution for kBM-Is that locates the boundary around $O(k \log(kn))$ additional points following $t$ initial queries. Consequently, to isolate these $O(k \log(kn))$ boundary points, the algorithm requires $O(kn)$ point queries in total. The study establishes lower bounds showing that algorithms cannot achieve better than $O(kn)$ queries regardless of how many boundary interval queries are employed. Furthermore, it proves that any algorithm utilizing $t$ unbounded point queries must necessarily perform $ \Omega(t)$ unbounded boundary interval queries to achieve a solution. Finally, the authors present a comprehensive algorithmic approach capable of solving kBM-IGS using exactly $O(kn)$ queries, contingent upon executing $O(kn)$ boundary interval queries.

Recent research has introduced the concept of using quantum-enhanced algorithms to train deep neural networks (Q-DNNs), proposing they could outperform traditional methods (DNNs) in specific machine learning tasks. This study rigorously evaluates that potential by demonstrating the theoretical and empirical advantages of Q-DNNs across three distinct classification scenarios. The first scenario involves linearly separable data, where we prove that the loss function for a Q-DNN is globally convex, guaranteeing that Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) will find the global optimum with a specific convergence rate. The second scenario addresses nonlinearly separable data, supported by experiments showing that Q-DNNs can achieve lower test error rates than their DNN counterparts. The third scenario examines noisy label data, experimentally confirming that Q-DNNs exhibit greater robustness compared to DNNs. Collectively, these findings underscore the promising potential of leveraging quantum computing advancements in artificial intelligence.

Additionally, this work establishes the monotonicity of eigenvalues when domains undergo specific types of smooth perturbations.

Rooted in these formal principles, we develop a time-efficient algorithm that generates an algorithmic trace true to the planning problem; the resulting plan quality matches existing state-of-the-art results. This study introduces a power system model that allows for a broad spectrum of economic and technical operational constraints, while also providing a sensitive analysis of how economic and technical parameters affect system outcomes. As a result, operators can assess the impact of specific elements essential for economic dispatch and analyze the sensitivity of power system models. The approach involves a non-linear optimization framework solved using the interior point method, with results validated against the IEEE 30-bus test system.

Software developers often articulate change requests in unstructured English, embedding essential details like execution environments, functional areas, and required skills within their text. However, current information extraction methods are hindered by the high variability in phrasing and vocabulary found in these requests. This study presents a new approach to automatically categoring change request attributes, specifically targeting a dataset of 1,000 items. The proposed method is a language-model-based, context-aware embedding system that integrates request-specific keywords with broader contextual change request information. By leveraging contextual embeddings, the system effectively identifies and incorporates significant keywords. This technique was evaluated against the SOON dataset and demonstrated superior performance compared to other state-of-the-art systems.

Colloidal gels are capable of undergoing reversible softening when subjected to ultrasonic vibrations. This paper presents a theoretical framework designed to explain this softening phenomenon and its subsequent re-hardening. The proposed model integrates a non-linear spring-based approach capable of explaining both the softening and re-hardening dynamics observed in experiments. Specifically, it attributes softening to a shift in particle coordination number driven by vibrational energy, alongside a frequency-dependent viscoelastic response arising from the time-dependent nature of these structural rearrangements. Furthermore, full hardening occurs once vibrations cease, as particles readjust to a lower energy state characterized by an increased coordination number. Crucially, re-hardening is characterized as a competition between particle readjustment and a vibrational diffusion coefficient that remains constant during oscillation.

This paper introduces and evaluates a document classification system designed to categorize research materials within Computer Science (CS) and Engineering. Our methodology centers on identifying mathematical entities to serve as features for training classifiers. Specifically, the proposed approach detects inline formulas, extracts high-value features from them, and employs a Random Forest model for categorization. Experimental results indicate that the system's accuracy is comparable to or exceeds that of systems relying on other features. Furthermore, the proposed method is computationally efficient, rendering it well-suited for processing large volumes of data.

This study introduces a new algorithm for the classically studied stable matching problem, specifically designed for scenarios with short preference lists. We demonstrate that when lists are restricted to a constant length of $L$, our algorithm achieves a running time of $O(NL \log NL + L^2 2^{2^L})$ for $N$ men and women. Although the algorithm's runtime is exponential relative to the exponent $L$ of preference lists, it exhibits only quasi-linear dependency on $N$ accompanied by a fixed overhead. This efficiency makes it particularly effective for small instances of rank lists, such as $L=5$ or $L=10$. We identify that our approach relies on the limited maximum depth of these lists, enabling the use of a graph structure where all connected components have a diameter bounded by $L/2$. By employing a divide-and-conquer strategy, we perform a stable matching between subsets of men and women and subsequently merge the results to produce the final matching.

The community currently lacks consensus on the precise metrics required to assess summary quality. Many existing evaluation metrics are either overly simplistic, such as relying on overlap-based metrics like ROUGE, or demand significant computational resources and large datasets for training, such as models that maximize log-likelihood. To address these gaps, we introduce SummScore, an efficient, computationally inexpensive metric that captures summary quality across four distinct dimensions: coherence, comprehensiveness, relevance, and informativeness. To validate our approach, we conducted extensive experiments on three large-scale datasets, demonstrating that our proposed metric outperforms traditional overlap metrics. Additionally, we performed a manual analysis to identify specific failure cases where SummScore exhibited limitations. To further support the research community, we have made our implementation code publicly available at https://github.com/EdinburghNLP/summscore.

This study introduces a novel approach for recovering sparse signals from underdetermined linear systems, leveraging the diagonal of a cross-correlation matrix. By addressing scenarios where a second, potentially noisy, set of measurements is available, our method exploits this cross-correlation to perform signal reconstruction. Theoretically, it is demonstrated that the proposed procedure achieves the optimal minimax error rate under certain conditions. Furthermore, comprehensive numerical simulations validate the superior performance of this method when compared to existing alternatives.

This study introduces a lightweight, camera-based framework for 3D object detection, leveraging the inherent redundancy of multi-camera sensor arrays. Our proposed method utilizes a single-frame detector trained on 3D bounding boxes like PointNetPP, which is then adapted to multiple perspectives using a view-point adaptation module grounded in graph attention mechanisms for feature fusion. This design ensures robustness in real-world deployments where sensors may fail, such as during LiDAR errors caused by heavy rain or snow. Additionally, it offers a cost-effective and maintenance-efficient solution for automotive 5G Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communication, which typically demands multiple LiDAR units. Validated on the nuScenes dataset, the model achieves a mAP of 20.6, outperforming the baseline by 3.1 points.

This study examines the propagation of a laser beam within a fluid undergoing convection and the resulting fluid dynamics, specifically comparing scenarios with and without heat transfer. The investigation focuses on how the laser induces localized heating, generating buoyancy-driven vortices, and analyzes the impact of this heat transfer on laser transmission as well as the subsequent energy distribution in the fluid. The analysis employs coupled governing equations for both fluid motion and thermal effects, solved numerically to visualize energy conversion from optical input to fluid motion and thermal output. Key parameters include the laser's incident angle and intensity along with the Rayleigh number, which quantifies the strength of the induced natural convection. Results demonstrate that including heat transfer significantly alters the characteristics of laser propagation and the spatial distribution of energy in the medium. Furthermore, the numerical simulations explore the energy conversion process from optical energy to thermal energy and finally to mechanical fluid energy. These findings offer insights into applications such as laser material processing, medical therapies, and fluid dynamics control, while also highlighting the complex interactions between optical forces, heat transfer mechanisms, and fluid motion in such systems.

Although design refactoring is a well-established area, design mining remains under-explored. Defined as identifying software design within source code, design mining serves as a foundational element for both understanding and building systems. This paper introduces a novel approach to automated design mining capable of handling legacy code. Our method begins by generating call graphs and flow graphs from source code, which are subsequently processed to derive high-level component and interaction data. These elements represent software components and their interconnections, respectively. Finally, this information is organized into a design graph and analyzed through a combination of rule-based and machine learning techniques to identify specific design patterns. Validated against a dataset of 130,, our approach demonstrated high precision in recovering both explicit and implicit design patterns, proving its effectiveness for analyzing both newly written code and pre-existing legacy systems.

Processing streams of massive data presents significant challenges for big data applications. While a micro-service architecture effectively addresses these processing demands by offering high scalability and fault tolerance, current implementations often suffer from performance bottlenecks due to the overhead of network communications. To overcome this, we introduce a novel in-order, in-place architecture designed to enhance performance by eliminating network latency. Our approach utilizes a new algorithm that synchronizes data across services while maintaining sequential integrity without relying on traditional distributed memory methods. We have developed a prototype system grounded in our proposed architecture and evaluated it against an existing system built upon the standard big data paradigm. The experimental results demonstrate that, under specific conditions, this new architecture can substantially outperform conventional solutions.
